title: Optional & Readonly Properties
summary: **Optional** (`?`) properties may be absent; **readonly** properties can't be reassigned after creation. Together with `Readonly<T>` and `readonly` arrays, they let you express *what may be missing* and *what must not change* — encoding intent the compiler enforces.

subtopics.title: Optional properties (?)
subtopics.explanation: A trailing `?` on a property means it may be omitted entirely. Its type becomes `T | undefined`, so reads must handle the missing case. Optional is for fields that genuinely might not exist, like a nickname or a cached value.
subtopics.example: interface User { id: number; nickname?: string; }

subtopics.title: Readonly properties
subtopics.explanation: The `readonly` modifier allows a property to be set once (at construction) but never reassigned afterwards. It's a compile-time guarantee against accidental mutation; the underlying JavaScript object is still mutable at runtime.
subtopics.example: interface Point { readonly x: number; readonly y: number; }

subtopics.title: Readonly<T> utility
subtopics.explanation: `Readonly<T>` is a built-in mapped type that makes every property of T readonly at once, without rewriting the interface. Great for freezing an existing shape — function parameters you promise not to mutate, for example.

subtopics.title: Readonly arrays and tuples
subtopics.explanation: `readonly T[]` (or `ReadonlyArray<T>`) forbids mutating methods like push/splice and index assignment. It signals 'I will only read this collection', preventing callers' data from being mutated unexpectedly.
subtopics.example: function sum(nums: readonly number[]) { /* nums.push(1) -> error */ }

subtopics.title: Optional vs explicit undefined union
subtopics.explanation: `x?: string` means the property may be *absent*; `x: string | undefined` means the property must be *present* but may hold undefined. With strict settings the difference matters: the union requires the key to exist (even as undefined), the `?` does not.
subtopics.example:
interface A { x?: string } // may omit
interface B { x: string | undefined } // must include x

subtopics.title: Immutability patterns
subtopics.explanation: Combine readonly properties, Readonly<T>, and readonly arrays to model immutable data and state. Pair them with `as const` for literal, deeply-narrowed constants. These patterns prevent shared state from being mutated by mistake.
subtopics.example: const ROUTES = ['/', '/about'] as const; // readonly tuple of literals

subtopics.title: When each matters
subtopics.explanation: Reach for optional when a field is legitimately not always there. Reach for readonly when a value must stay stable after creation — config, ids, props, redux-style state. Using both intentionally turns the type into living documentation of your data's rules.
subtopics.example: interface Props { readonly id: number; title?: string; }

foundations.overview: Optional and readonly are two property modifiers that let object types express more than just 'this field is a string'. Optional (?) captures fields that may be absent; readonly captures fields that must not be reassigned. Plus the Readonly<T> utility and readonly arrays extend immutability to whole shapes and collections.
foundations.formalDefinition: An optional member (name?: T) may be omitted and has type T | undefined when read. A readonly member can be assigned only during initialization and cannot be reassigned afterwards; the constraint is enforced by the compiler, not at runtime.
foundations.whyItMatters: These modifiers encode the rules of your data — what can be missing, what must stay constant — so the compiler enforces them. They're heavily used in React props and state, and interviewers probe the optional-vs-undefined distinction and the limits of compile-time immutability.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of ? as 'may be skipped' and readonly as 'set once, never reset'. Readonly<T> is 'lock the whole shape'; readonly T[] is 'lock the collection'.
foundations.browserPerspective: Both modifiers are erased at compile time. At runtime the object is an ordinary, fully mutable JavaScript object — readonly is not Object.freeze. For runtime immutability you must freeze explicitly.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Optional props (title?: string), readonly ids and config, Readonly<Props> in components, and readonly arrays for data you only iterate are everyday uses.
foundations.businessImpact: Marking fields readonly prevents a class of mutation bugs (shared state changed unexpectedly) that are hard to trace in production, reducing incident time and risk.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Modifiers make data contracts explicit, so engineers know at a glance which fields are stable and which may be missing — fewer defensive checks, safer refactors.
foundations.performanceImpact: No runtime cost (erased). Choosing readonly types can even help engines and reviewers reason about code, but the immutability itself is compile-time only.
commonUseCases: Optional component props and config fields
readonly ids and other set-once values
Readonly<T> for parameters you promise not to mutate
readonly arrays for collections you only read

commonMisconceptions.myth: readonly makes the object immutable at runtime.
commonMisconceptions.reality: readonly is compile-time only; the runtime object is still mutable. Use Object.freeze for real runtime immutability.

commonMisconceptions.myth: x?: T and x: T | undefined are the same.
commonMisconceptions.reality: ? allows the property to be absent; the union requires the property to be present (possibly holding undefined). Under exactOptionalPropertyTypes they differ further.

config.intro: Trace a type with { readonly id: number; nickname?: string } as you read and write its fields.

steps.name: Declare modifiers
steps.detail: interface User { readonly id: number; nickname?: string } marks id as set-once and nickname as possibly-absent.

steps.name: Construct the object
steps.detail: const u: User = { id: 1 } is valid — nickname may be omitted, id is provided.

steps.name: Read the optional field
steps.detail: u.nickname has type string | undefined, so TypeScript requires a guard before using it.

steps.name: Remember runtime reality
steps.detail: All checks are erased; at runtime the object is mutable JS — readonly is a promise to the compiler only.

debuggingLab.title: Mutating data the caller didn't expect
debuggingLab.symptom: A helper sorts an array in place, silently mutating the caller's original list and corrupting other views of the data.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Typing the parameter as number[] allows in-place mutation. sort() reorders the caller's array. Declaring it readonly number[] would make the sort() call a compile error, forcing a non-mutating copy and protecting the caller's data.
commonMistakes: Assuming array methods like sort/reverse return a new array — they mutate in place.
Typing parameters as mutable arrays when the function only needs to read them.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Type the parameter as readonly number[] and copy before sorting so the caller's array is untouched.

theory.question: What is the difference between an optional property (x?: T) and a required property typed T | undefined?
theory.directAnswer: x?: T means the property may be entirely absent — you can omit the key. x: T | undefined means the key must be present, but it may hold undefined. With default settings both let you read undefined, but the union forces you to include the key (even as undefined), while ? lets you leave it out. Under exactOptionalPropertyTypes the distinction tightens further.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two ways a value can be 'missing': an absent key versus a present key holding undefined.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: They model different intents — truly optional fields vs. fields that must be acknowledged even when empty.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler treats ? as 'key may not exist'; the union treats undefined as a normal value of a required member.

theory.whyImportant: It's a classic interview distinction and affects API ergonomics — whether callers can omit a field or must pass undefined.
theory.realWorldExample: A required callback that may be cleared is often onChange: Fn | undefined (must be provided), while a rarely-used flag is debug?: boolean (omittable).

nestedTopics.title: exactOptionalPropertyTypes
nestedTopics.explanation: This strict flag stops ? properties from being explicitly set to undefined, sharpening the difference.

nestedTopics.title: Reading both
nestedTopics.explanation: Both surface as T | undefined when read, so guards look similar at the use site.

followUps.question: Which should an API prefer?
followUps.answer: Use ? when callers should be able to omit the field; use the union when the field must be present but may be empty/cleared.

theory.question: Does readonly make an object immutable at runtime? How would you achieve real runtime immutability?
theory.directAnswer: No — readonly is a compile-time check only. It stops you from reassigning a property in TypeScript, but the emitted JavaScript object is fully mutable; another piece of code (or any cast) can change it. For genuine runtime immutability, use Object.freeze (shallow) or a deep-freeze utility, and treat readonly as documentation plus a compiler guard.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: readonly is a type-system modifier; Object.freeze is a runtime operation.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: readonly catches accidental reassignment during development with zero runtime cost; freeze enforces immutability when untrusted code shares the object.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: readonly is erased at emit. Object.freeze sets the object non-writable/non-configurable so writes silently fail (or throw in strict mode).

theory.whyImportant: Confusing compile-time and runtime guarantees is a common bug source and a frequent interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: Redux state is typed Readonly for safety in the editor, but the real protection against mutation comes from reducers returning new objects, not from readonly itself.

nestedTopics.title: Object.freeze is shallow
nestedTopics.explanation: Nested objects remain mutable; you need a deep freeze for full immutability.

nestedTopics.title: as const
nestedTopics.explanation: Makes a literal deeply readonly at compile time, useful for constant data.

followUps.question: Can you bypass readonly?
followUps.answer: Yes — a type assertion or untyped JavaScript can mutate the object, because readonly has no runtime presence.

scenario.question: A utility function is mutating arrays passed in by callers, causing hard-to-trace bugs across the app. How do you use the type system to prevent this?
scenario.directAnswer: Type the parameters as readonly T[] (or ReadonlyArray<T>). That makes mutating methods (push, splice, sort, index assignment) compile errors inside the function, forcing the author to copy before transforming. The caller's array is then provably untouched, and the readonly type also documents the function's contract.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Using readonly arrays to forbid in-place mutation of inputs.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Mutable parameters let functions secretly change shared data, producing spooky action at a distance.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: readonly T[] removes mutating members from the type, so any mutation attempt fails to compile; you copy ([...arr]) to transform.

scenario.whyImportant: Shared-mutation bugs are notoriously hard to debug; this shows the candidate can prevent whole bug classes with types.

nestedTopics.title: Copy-then-transform
nestedTopics.explanation: Spread or slice to a new array before sort/map/filter.

nestedTopics.title: Readonly<T> for objects
nestedTopics.explanation: The same idea for object parameters you promise not to mutate.

followUps.question: Does readonly array stop the caller from mutating their own array elsewhere?
followUps.answer: No — it only constrains the function's view. The caller still owns a mutable array; readonly just prevents this function from mutating it.

coding.question: Write a function withDefaults that takes a Readonly config with required url and optional timeout/retries, and returns a fully-populated config applying defaults — without mutating the input.
coding.thoughtProcess: The input is Readonly<Config> so I can't mutate it; I'll build a new object. timeout and retries are optional (number | undefined), so I use ?? to apply defaults. The return type has those fields required since defaults guarantee they exist.
coding.lineByLine: Config marks timeout and retries optional; FullConfig makes them required. The parameter is Readonly<Config>, so attempting cfg.timeout = ... would not compile. We return a brand-new object, applying ?? defaults for the optional fields, leaving the input untouched.

alternativeApproaches.title: Spread with defaults
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Spread the input over a defaults object; order matters so caller values win.
alternativeApproaches.code:
const DEFAULTS = { timeout: 5000, retries: 3 };
function withDefaults(cfg: Readonly<Config>) { return { ...DEFAULTS, ...cfg }; }

followUps.question: Why return a new object instead of editing the input?
followUps.answer: Because Readonly<Config> forbids mutation and, more importantly, mutating shared input causes side effects for the caller.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Optional and readonly modifiers encode data contracts across layers: readonly ids and config at the boundary, optional fields for partial DTOs, and Readonly<T> on props/state to signal one-way data flow.
productionDeepDive.performance: All modifiers are erased — zero runtime cost. Real runtime immutability via Object.freeze has a small cost and is usually reserved for shared constants or debug builds.
productionDeepDive.security: readonly does not protect against malicious or buggy runtime mutation; it's a development aid. For data that must not change at runtime (e.g. frozen config), use Object.freeze and validate inputs.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Consistent use of Readonly<T> and readonly arrays in shared utilities prevents accidental mutation bugs from spreading as more code reuses the same data structures.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Marking fields optional vs required and readonly vs mutable turns types into documentation of the data's rules, making intent obvious during reviews and refactors.
productionDeepDive.observability: tsc surfaces readonly violations and unhandled optional fields in the editor and CI; strict flags like strictNullChecks and exactOptionalPropertyTypes tighten the net.

caseStudies.problem: Accidental state mutation caused stale UI and untraceable bugs.
caseStudies.solution: Type state as Readonly and enforce returning new objects from reducers; optionally freeze in development.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More copying and discipline vs. predictable, debuggable state.
caseStudies.lessons: readonly types document intent, but runtime immutability still requires non-mutating update patterns.

keyTakeaways: Optional (?) marks a property as possibly absent; reading it yields T | undefined, so you must guard.
readonly allows a property to be set once and never reassigned — enforced only at compile time.
Readonly<T> locks an entire shape, and readonly T[] forbids mutating an array (push/sort/etc.).
x?: T (may be absent) differs from x: T | undefined (must be present, may be undefined).
readonly is not runtime immutability — use Object.freeze and non-mutating updates for that.
